summary: Lavenham clothier's son who emigrated to New England and became one of Watertown, Massachusetts's largest landowners; John's 11th-great-grandfather.
bio:
William Hammond was baptized at Lavenham in Suffolk on 30 October 1575, 'William, son of Thomas Hamond' in the parish register. His father died when William was fourteen, and his mother remarried within five months. On 9 June 1605 he married Elizabeth Paine at Lavenham, where their children William (1607), Anne (1609), John (1611), Anna (1616), Thomas (1618) and John (1626) were baptized, probably along with 'Marie', baptized in 1623, who is thought to be the daughter Sarah. In England he stood surety for the debts of his son William.

He sailed for New England in the 1630s; his wife followed on the Francis in April 1634 with three of the children. He was at Scituate before 1636 and became a freeman of Watertown in 1636, where he was one of the largest landowners, with 331 acres and an estate valued at £457. The Rev. George Phillips called him 'my brother Hammond'. In 1661 the houses of 'old Warren and Goodman Hammond' were ordered searched for Quakers; the John Warren concerned had emigrated with the Hammonds and had been their neighbour on Hall Street in Melford.

His will, dated July 1662 and proved on 16 December 1672, left 'to Adam Smith, son of daughter, Sarah, if he behave obediently to my wife after my decease, one mare colt and £20' and 'to daughter, Sarah Smith, £5', and penalized his grandson Thomas if he contested it. He died at Watertown before 16 December 1672. Through the Hammonds John is related to Col. John F. Farnsworth and S. D. Warren, 6th cousins six times removed, and to Samuel D. Warren II, Edward Perry Warren, Henry Clarke Warren, Fiske Warren and Cornelia Warren, 7th cousins five times removed.
funFacts: Left his grandson Adam Smith a colt 'if he behave obediently'.
His house was searched for Quakers in 1661.
